[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of U.S. states or counties with differential immigration policy changes (e.g., post-2016 or post-2020) matched to wage records from the Current Population Survey or Quarterly Workforce Indicators, focusing on wage dispersion between high-skill and low-skill native workers over 3-5 year windows. — Directly tests the causal link by comparing jurisdictions that tightened restrictions against those that did not, isolating the effect on wage polarization while controlling for other economic factors.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market simulation model calibrated to a representative developed economy (e.g., U.S. or Germany) with endogenous skill supply, firm demand, and immigration policy parameters, varying the restrictiveness of low-skill immigration and observing native wage ratios. — Provides a controlled environment to isolate the hypothesized mechanism (reduced competition in low-skill sectors vs. increased demand for high-skill substitutes) and test sensitivity to assumptions about substitutability and market frictions.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing studies on immigration policy changes and native wage effects, focusing on papers that separately estimate impacts on high-skill and low-skill workers (e.g., Borjas, 2003; Card, 2009; Peri, 2012) and extract effect sizes for wage polarization. — Synthesizes available empirical evidence to assess overall support for the hypothesis, identify inconsistent findings, and highlight gaps in the literature (e.g., lack of medium-term studies).

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data on employment and wage trends in low-skill sectors (e.g., agriculture, hospitality, construction) before and after 2017-2023 policy changes, combined with administrative data on visa issuance and enforcement actions — Provides direct quantitative evidence on whether restrictive policies reduced low-skill labor supply and whether such reductions correlate with slower job growth or output in essential sectors, enabling causal inference via difference-in-differences or panel regression.

[PATH:literature] Peer-reviewed studies from NBER or IZA on the economic effects of immigration restrictions (e.g., on H-2A/ H-2B visa caps, public charge rule), focusing on labor shortages, firm productivity, and local economic stagnation — Synthesizes existing empirical findings to assess whether the hypothesized mechanism (low-skill worker scarcity → stagnation) is supported across multiple contexts, accounting for confounding factors like automation or wage adjustments.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor market complementarity and production functions (e.g., Cobb-Douglas with low- and high-skill labor) calibrated to US data, simulating the impact of a reduction in low-skill immigration on GDP growth and sectoral output — Tests the logical consistency of the hypothesis under standard economic assumptions, providing a counterfactual benchmark against which empirical data can be compared and identifying conditions under which the effect may be mitigated or amplified.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal surveys of R&D firms (e.g., NSF Business R&D and Innovation Survey) to measure changes in hiring of foreign high-skilled workers and knowledge spillover metrics (e.g., co-invention networks, cross-firm citations) after 2010 — Provides firm-level evidence on whether restrictive policies reduce innovation through reduced collaboration and knowledge transfer, not just individual inventor output.

[PATH:theoretical] Economic models of endogenous innovation with heterogeneous agents (e.g., extended Jones or Romer models) calibrated to US high-skill immigration data — Simulates the counterfactual of no policy change to isolate the causal effect of immigration restrictions on aggregate patenting and innovation, accounting for general equilibrium effects.

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, cross-referenced with H-1B visa issuance data from USCIS — Analyzing short-term wage changes in high-skill occupations (e.g., software developers, engineers) before and after restrictive policy changes (e.g., H-1B denial rate increases) can isolate the effect of reduced labor supply on domestic wages. Controlling for industry demand shifts would help confirm or refute the wage-boost claim.

[PATH:literature] National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) working papers on immigration and innovation, e.g., Kerr & Lincoln (2010) and Peri (2012) — Existing studies find that high-skill immigrants complement domestic workers and spur innovation; restrictive policies may reduce patenting and R&D activity. Reviewing this literature will test the hypothesis that restricting immigration encourages domestic innovation, as the evidence often points to the opposite effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market model calibrated to US high-skill sectors, incorporating immigration policy shocks — A dynamic general equilibrium model can simulate the short-term (1-3 year) impact of reduced high-skill immigration on domestic labor demand, wages, and innovation incentives. This would clarify the causal mechanisms and quantify the net effect, addressing the disputed confidence level.
